question: Which part of the gastrointestinal tract is responsible for the absorption of most nutrients?
explanation: The small intestine has specialized structures that make it the primary site for nutrient uptake in the digestive system. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the primary purpose of gastrointestinal absorption?

options.A: To move digested food into the blood or lymph
options.B: To produce digestive enzymes for the stomach
options.C: To eliminate waste products from the body
options.D: To break down large food molecules into smaller pieces

explanation: Absorption is the transfer of processed nutrients from the gut lumen into the circulatory and lymphatic systems for body use. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h1)

question: What name is given to the tiny, microscopic projections on the surface of intestinal absorptive cells?
explanation: Microvilli form a brush border on intestinal cells, which greatly increases the surface area available for taking in nutrients. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h2)

question: How do circular folds inside the small intestine help with nutrient absorption?

options.A: They produce bile acids to break down fats
options.B: They directly pump glucose across the cell membrane
options.C: They slow down the movement of digested food to allow more time for uptake
options.D: They prevent bacteria from entering the bloodstream

explanation: The circular folds cause digesting food to spiral through the tract, ensuring it stays in contact with the absorptive surface longer. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which transport process uses cellular energy to move substances against a concentration gradient?
explanation: Active transport uses energy to move molecules from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why can fat-soluble molecules pass easily through the cell membrane using simple diffusion?

options.A: Because they require specialized carrier proteins
options.B: Because they are too large to fit through pores
options.C: Because the cell membrane is made of a lipid layer
options.D: Because they must be pumped using ATP energy

explanation: Because fat-soluble substances mix well with fats, they pass easily through the fatty interior of the cell membrane without needing extra help. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the name of the packaged fat droplets that enter the lymphatic system after fat digestion?
explanation: Intestinal cells package reassembled fats with proteins into chylomicrons so they can safely enter the lymphatic vessels. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h4)

question: What role do bile salts play in the digestion and absorption of dietary fats?

options.A: They digest carbohydrates into simple sugars
options.B: They break down large fat drops into tiny droplets
options.C: They actively pump fatty acids across the brush border
options.D: They convert proteins into usable amino acids

explanation: Bile salts break large fat masses into tiny droplets, making it possible for digestive enzymes to work and for fats to be absorbed. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which substance must bind to Vitamin B12 in the stomach to enable its absorption further down the gut?
explanation: Intrinsic factor is produced by cells in the stomach and is required for Vitamin B12 absorption further down the tract. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h5)

question: How do fat-soluble vitamins get absorbed across the intestinal lining?

options.A: They cross the membrane only through endocytosis
options.B: They travel inside fat droplets and are absorbed passively
options.C: They bind exclusively to intrinsic factor in the duodenum
options.D: They require specific active transport pumps driven by ATP

explanation: Because they dissolve in fats, vitamins A, D, E, and K follow the same absorption pathway as dietary fats. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h5)

question: By what physical process does water move across the intestinal epithelium?
explanation: Water moves passively across membranes from areas of low solute concentration to high solute concentration through osmosis. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary driving force that pulls water out of the intestinal lumen?

options.A: The pumping action of the gastric glands
options.B: The pulling effect created by absorbed solutes and salts
options.C: Secretion of bile acids into the duodenum
options.D: Direct muscular contractions of the intestinal wall

explanation: As sodium and other nutrients are actively absorbed, they create an osmotic pull that draws water along with them. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which blood vessel network carries absorbed water-soluble nutrients directly to the liver?
explanation: The hepatic portal vein delivers blood containing absorbed sugars and amino acids straight to the liver for processing. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why do dietary fats enter the lymphatic system rather than directly into blood capillaries?

options.A: Because lymphatic vessels contain active pumps for lipids
options.B: Because the liver cannot process any form of dietary fat
options.C: Because digested fat particles are too large to pass through blood capillary walls
options.D: Because fat molecules are destroyed by blood enzymes

explanation: Fat particles are bulky and must enter the more permeable lacteals of the lymphatic system instead. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the term for fatty, pale, and foul-smelling stools caused by unabsorbed dietary fats?
explanation: Steatorrhea occurs when fats cannot be properly digested or absorbed, leading to high fat content in the stool. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h8)

question: A pregnant woman presents with chronic diarrhea, severe fatigue, and pale bulky stools that float. Which condition should a midwife suspect?
explanation: Fatty floating stools and fatigue point toward an inability to absorb nutrients and fats properly. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h8)
